input: It is worth noting that the two groups report substantially different pressure drop values for what is, on the surface, the same class of material, and closer examination of their test conditions reveals differences that help to explain the discrepancy. The higher values came from beds of loose powder, where the bed producing the drop is finer and more closely packed than any formed body the process will contain; the lower values came from pellets of the benchmark material in a shallow layer, where the reported drop includes the resistance of the holder and its supports, which the authors do not separate from the bed. The two measurements are therefore not strictly measuring the same thing, and the conflict is in part a conflict of test pieces. Bed depth plays a role as well, since the powder beds were deep relative to their diameter, so distribution and wall effects enter the two results differently. Each group reports the uptake at which the drop was measured; the pellet group's loadings sit closer to the working loading of the separation, and its tests cover the range of gas rates the duty requires, where the powder tests ran below that range. IAST is common to both groups' calculations and explains none of the difference. On the match of form and loading, the pellet values would appear to be the better guide for design, although the preference is a limited one: it holds for the benchmark material as formed pellets, at loadings near the working loading. A change of form, a finer feed, or a duty at loadings outside the tested range removes that ground, and neither set of values then carries over without a fresh measurement on the material in the form the duty will use.

IAST is common to both groups' calculations and explains none of the difference.
